extracted.intended_audience: school teachers (especially young or beginning teachers); school principals; educators in public and private elementary/academy settings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for running and improving a school: classroom procedure, discipline, religious instruction, and when/how to introduce innovations or new texts. Aimed at advising young teachers how to conduct daily school life without sacrificing core duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: School court procedure and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A mock court is held after school to try minor offenses among pupils, with an appointed jury and witnesses; sessions are held out of school hours and not entrusted with serious business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark off a precinct within which no one may enter; summon accused and witnesses; appoint two bystanders as jury; allow the accused to inspect the indictment; hear witnesses and defence; jury writes 'guilty' or 'not guilty'; if sentenced, punishment should be confinement to seat during a recess or other slight but real penalty. The court's influence is 'in a double way; making amusement, and preserving order.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences in school court: real but slight
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sentence pronounced should be something real though always slight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use penalties that require 'slight effort or sacrifice, for the public good' (e.g., confinement to seat during part of recess) so the court is taken seriously without harshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious instruction: primary aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The school should exert a decided moral and religious influence over pupils' hearts, gently and openly, to promote piety and conscientious conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to have pupils 'feel their accountability to God', explore their hearts, seek forgiveness through Christian principle, and 'begin to act from Christian principle' so that conscience and moral principle 'reign here.' The influence should be 'gentle and alluring' rather than coercive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious exercises in school (daily practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short devotional exercises integrated into regular school routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open and close the school with a very short prayer and one or two verses of a hymn; occasionally occupy 10–15 minutes at a general exercise or close of school to give instruction on practical religious duty, sometimes suggested by scripture but more commonly by other means (e.g., submitted questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-wrapper practice for collective religious inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A wrapper at the teacher's desk receives scholars' written questions or remarks on moral/religious duty for public treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow any pupil to deposit questions, anecdotes, or short statements of fact for the teacher to address in general exercises; makes religious instruction participatory and responsive to pupils' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary Saturday religious meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A longer, voluntary religious meeting held Saturday afternoons for those interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended for those who can attend with parental approval; instruction should be 'plain, direct, and practical,' run about half an hour starting at 3:30 p.m.; attendance is voluntary and pupils may invite friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal religious instruction (pupil-initiated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private, written communications from pupils requesting personal religious advice; teacher replies briefly and concisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pupils should begin these communications; the teacher generally will not initiate private religious correspondence (except rare peculiar cases). Written replies allow pupils to reread and reflect; teacher's time is limited so answers are short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious instruction philosophy: win, not compel
rubrics_metrics.description: All means of religious instruction should 'win and allure, not to compel'; default exposure is only regular devotional exercises; other activities are private and voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not coerce attendance or personal counsel; avoid reproach or threatening—leave pupils free to choose while making help and sympathizers available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against excessive scheming and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: While ingenuity and enterprise are valuable, an over-eagerness for novel schemes can waste time and derail a teacher from essential duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between genuine improvements (which should be encouraged) and whimsical innovations sustained only by original enthusiasm. Avoid letting a single new idea expand into an obsession that distracts from present work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the novelty effect
rubrics_metrics.description: New methods often appear successful mainly because they are new and awaken interest, not because they are intrinsically superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that temporary gains from novelty may fade; treat new plans as means to enliven study, not as proven permanent replacements. Inspect whether improvements persist when novelty wears off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage variety in details but preserve core objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise ingenuity to provide variety in the minute details of daily study while keeping the leading objects and measures steady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variety combats dull routine, but should not replace or undermine the school's fundamental aims and consistent practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1: Study the existing school system thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before proposing broad changes, examine the system of public and private schools as constituted until you fully understand its organization and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate the system's provision for various population classes; note this refers to organizational completeness rather than internal management, which remains a field for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2: Gauge your readiness for reform (age, experience, standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think change is necessary, consider whether your age, experience, and standing as an instructor justify confidence in your opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young enthusiasm may overvalue minor differences; be self-critical about whether your perspective mistakes novelty for essential improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3: Consider sustainability of a new institution
rubrics_metrics.description: If planning a new establishment, consider whether it can be carried on after you leave and whether ordinary successors can maintain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the risk of poor imitations and the responsibility you bear for consequences; recognize that institutions founded on peculiar personal notions may fail in others' hands and could do indirect harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5: Before introducing a new study, consider the school's true object
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everything important in itself belongs in school; a school's purpose is limited and specific, not to supplant parental responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the branch is properly an object for the institution, remembering schools should pursue a comparatively small part of general education that benefits from association.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6: Avoid excessive complexity; assess teacher capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Before adding a branch, consider whether its introduction (and that of other equally claiming branches) will make common schools too complex and whether ordinary teachers can teach it well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether it will draw the teacher's attention from essential duties; favor simplicity and remember public schools' primary design: 'teaching the whole population to read, write, and calculate.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 7: When preparing a school-book, test general usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a textbook suited to your personal method will be superior for general use; many textbooks succeed only in their inventor's hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether your book is 'for general use' so superior to existing works that teachers will adopt it; beware that a method adapted to your idiosyncrasies may fail in ordinary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improving existing institutions over isolated experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: By working within regularly organized schools, a teacher of talent elevates the whole system more than by founding a fanciful isolated institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful teachers in established institutions influence others broadly; starting a new, idiosyncratic establishment may confine positive effects and encourage only weak imitators.
